lish infantry (see ''thousand'' and ''hundred''). The commander of a twenty was called ''vintiner''.

'''Twenty-first rule.''' See ''rule''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Twenty-five Articles.''' See ''article''.

'''twenty-fold''' (twen′ti-fōld), ''a.'' [< ''twenty'' + ''-fold''.] Twenty times as many.

'''twenty-four''' (twen′ti-fōr′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Four more than twenty: a cardinal numeral. —{{smaller|'''Twenty-four hours,''' a day, as consisting of so many hours.}}
{{smaller block|Botanists may find it worth while to observe if it [the Martagon lily] smells offensively at any time during the ''twenty-four hours.''
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 193.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The number made up of four and twenty.—'''2.''' A symbol representing this number, as 24, XXIV, or xxiv.—'''3.''' ''pl.'' In ''printing'': (''a'') A form of composed type or plates containing twenty-four pages properly arranged for printing and folding in consecutive order. (''b'') A sheet of paper printed from a form arranged as above described. (''c'') A book made up of sections of twenty-four pages.
{{smaller block|I have observed that the author of a folio . . . sets himself above the author of a quarto; the author of a quarto above the author of an octavo; and so on, by a gradual descent and subordination, to an author in ''twenty-fours.''
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 529.}}}}

'''twentyfour-mo''' (twen′ti-fōr′mō), ''n.'' [An English reading of 24''mo'', which stands for XXIV''mo'', i. e. L. (''in'') ''vicesimo quarto'', ‘in twentyfourth’; cf. ''twelvemo'', ''duodecimo'', etc.] '''1.''' A leaf from a sheet of paper regularly folded for a book in
readings.c2s3:
twenty-four equal parts. {{smaller|When the size of paper is not named, it is supposed to be a medium 24mo, of which the untrimmed leaf is about 3⅝ by 5¼ inches.}} '''2.''' A book made up of leaves folded in twenty-four equal parts.

Usually written 24''mo''.

'''twentymo''' (twen′ti-mō), ''n.'' [Cf. ''twentyfourmo.''] A sheet regularly folded to make twenty leaves of uniform size. Written shortly 20''mo''. ''C. T. Jacobi'', Printers’ Vocab.

'''twenty-second''' (twen′ti-sek′ond), ''n.'' In ''music'', a tone distant three octaves from a given tone, or the interval between two such tones; a triple octave.

'''’twere''' (twėr). A contraction of ''it were''.
{{smaller block|You are so ridiculously unworthy that ’''twere'' a Folly to reprove you with a serious Look.
{{right|''Etherege'', She-Would if She Could, iv. 2.}}}}

'''twey†''', '''tweyn†''', '''tweyfold†'''. See ''twain'', ''twofold''.

'''twi-'''. [Also ''twy-''; < ME. ''twi-'', < AS. ''twi-'' = OFries. ''twi-'' = D. ''twee-'' = MLG. ''twi-'', ''twe-'', LG. ''twe-'' = OHG. MHG. ''zwi-'', G. ''zwie-'' = Icel. ''tvī'', a combining form of AS. ''twā'', etc., E. ''two'': see ''two'', and cf. ''bi-''<sup>2</sup>, ''di-''<sup>2</sup>.] A prefix of Anglo-Saxon origin, a form of ''two'' in composition. It occurs in ''twibill'', ''twiblade'', ''twifallow'', ''twifold'', ''twilight'', etc.

'''twibill''' (twī′bil), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''twibil'', ''twybill'', ''twybil'', ''twyble''; < ME. ''twibil'', ''twyble'', < AS. ''twibill'', < ''twi-'', two, + ''bill'', a bill: see ''twi-'' and ''bill''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' A double-bladed battle-ax, especially that carried by the Northern nations. {{smaller|Such battle-axes are often mentioned in literature, although but few heads of double axes have been found among thousands of other types. Compare ''Danish ax'' (under ''Danish''), and ''ax''.}}

standing of the word. See the quotation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where ''Twibil'' hung, with basket-hilt,
Grown rusty now, but had been gilt.</poem>
{{right|''Cotton'', Scarronides, iv.}}}}
'''3.''' A kind of double ax; a kind of mattock the blade of which has one end shaped like an ax and the other like an adz.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit toles moo
The mattok, ''twyble'', picoys, forth to goo.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 42.}}
<poem>She learn’d the churlish axe and ''twybill'' to prepare,
To steel the coulter’s edge, and sharp the furrowing share.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xviii. 77.}}}}
'''4.''' A mortising-tool.
{{smaller block|A ''twybill'', which is a toole wherewith carpenters make mortaises. ''Nomenclator.'' (''Nares.'')}}
'''5.''' A reaping-hook. ''Drayton.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')—'''6†.''' Same as ''roaring boy'' (see ''roaring'').
{{smaller block|Those lawless ruffians who, to the disgrace of the city, under the various names of Mohawks, . . . ''Twibills'', . . . etc., infested the streets, . . . from the days of Elizabeth down to the beginning of the last century.
{{right|''Gifford'', note in Ford’s Sun’s Darling, i. 1.}}}}

'''twibilled''' (twī′bild), ''a.'' [< ''twibill'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Armed with a twibill or twibills.
{{smaller block|<poem>But if in this reign
The halberted train
Or the constable should rebel,
And make this ''twybill’d'' militia to swell.</poem>
{{right|''Loyal Songs.'' (''Mason’s Supp. to Johnson.'')}}}}

'''twiblade''' (twī′blād), ''n.'' [Also ''twyblade''; < ''twi-'' + ''blade''.] Same as ''twayblade''.

'''twice''' (twīs), ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. ''twise''; < ME. ''twies'', ''twiȝes'', < AS. ''twiges'' (= MLG. ''twiges'', ''twies'' = MHG. ''zwies''), with adv. gen. ''-es'', < AS. ''twiwa'', ME. ''twie'', twice: see ''twie''.] '''1.''' Two times; on
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>Please but your worship now
To take three drops of the rich water with you,
I’ll undertake your man shall cure you, sir,
''At twice'' i’ your own chamber.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, iv. 2.}}}}

'''Twice-laid rope.''' See ''rope''<sup>1</sup>.

'''twice†''' (twīs), ''a.'' [< ''twice, adv.''] Occurring twice.
{{smaller block|And, more to our sorrow, we heard of the ''twice'' returne of the Paragon, that now the third time was sent vs three moneths agoe.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 236.}}}}

'''twicer''' (twī′sėr), ''n.'' [< ''twice'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A typographer who works at both composition and presswork. [Eng.]

'''twice-stabbed''' (twīs′stabd), ''a.'' In ''entom.'', having two red marks like stabs on the dark ground of the elytra: as, the ''twice-stabbed'' ladybird, ''Chilocorus bivulnerus.''

'''twice-told''' (twīs′tōld), ''a.'' Told or related twice; hence, trite; hackneyed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Life is as tedious as a ''twice-told'' tale
Vexing the dull ear of a drowsy man.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 4. 108.}}}}

'''twice-writhen''' (twīs′riᴛ̵ʜ″n), ''n.'' The bistort, ''Polygonum Bistorta.'' See ''Polygonum.''

'''twich†''', '''twicher†'''. Old spellings of ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''twitcher.''

'''twichild†''' (twī′chīld), ''a.'' [Also ''twychild''; < ''twi-'' + ''child.''] Being in second childhood. Compare ''twitchel''<sup>2</sup>.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|Twelfth-day|6550|twichild}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|view is to do honour to the three wise men, or, as they are more generally denominated, the three kings.
{{right|''Chambers’s Book of Days'', I. 62.}}}}

'''Twelfth-night''' (twelfth′nīt), ''n.'' The eve of the festival of the Epiphany. {{smaller|Many social rites and ceremonies have long been connected with Twelfth-night. See ''bean-feast'', 2, ''Twelfth-cake''.—'''Twelfth-night cards''', a series of cards representing different characters to be assumed by the persons to whom the different cards fall, during the Twelfth-night celebration. The characters indicated, usually those of king, queen, ministers, maids of honor, or ludicrous or grotesque personages, are hence known as ''Twelfth-night characters''.}}
{{smaller block|John Britton, in his Autobiography, tells us he “suggested and wrote a series of ''Twelfth-Night Characters'', to be printed on cards, placed in a bag, and drawn out at parties on the memorable and merry evening. . . . They were sold in small packets to pastry-cooks.”
{{right|''Chambers’s Book of Days'', I. 64.}}}}

'''Twelfth-tide''' (twelfth′tīd), ''n.'' The time or festival of Twelfth-day.
{{smaller block|<poem>Come then, come then, and let us bring
Unto our prettie ''Twelfth-Tide'' King
Each one his severall offering.</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', Thi Star-song: a Caroll to the King.}}}}

'''twell''' (twel), ''prep.'' and ''conj.'' A dialectal variant of ''till''<sup>2</sup>.

'''twelve''' (twelv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''twelve'', ''twelf'', < AS. ''twelf'', ''twelfe'' = OS. ''twelif'' = OFries. ''twelf'', ''twelef'', ''twilif'' = D. ''twaalf'' = MLG. ''twelf'', ''twelef'', ''twolf'', LG. ''twolf'', ''twolve'' = OHG. ''zwelif'', MHG. ''zwelif'', ''zwelf'', G. ''zwölf'' = Icel. ''tolf'' = Sw. ''tolf'' = Dan. ''tolv'' = Goth. ''twalif'', twelve; < AS. ''twā'', etc., two, + ''-lif'', an element found also in ''eleven'', q. v.] '''I.''' ''a.'' One more than eleven; twice six, or three times four: a cardinal numeral.—'''Lady with twelve flounces.''' {{smaller|See ''lady''.}}—'''Twelve Men.''' {{smaller|Same as ''dozine''.}}—'''Twelve Tables.''' {{smaller|See ''table''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The number made up of ten and two; a dozen.—'''2.''' A symbol representing this number, as 12, XII, or xii.—'''3.''' ''pl.'' Same as ''duodecimo.''

{{smaller block|The nation must then have consisted of young readers, when a diminutive volume in ''twelves'' was deemed to be overlong.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., I. 312.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Broad twelves,''' a duodecimo leaf of extra width, of medium size, about 5¼ inches wide by 7½ inches long.—'''Long twelves,''' an oblong sheet of paper, folded for eight pages in its greater length and in three pages for its shorter length. Of medium size, it is about 4¼ inches wide and 8 inches long.—'''Quorum of twelve.''' See ''quorum.''—'''Square twelves,''' an arrangement of duodecimo pages for a sheet nearly square, in which the folded sheet has six pages in width and four pages in length.—'''The Twelve,''' the twelve apostles. See ''apostle'', 1.}}

{{smaller block|And Judas Iscariot, one of ''the twelve'', went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them.
{{right|Mark xiv. 10.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Twelve-day writ.''' See ''writ.''}}

'''twelvemo''' (twelv′mō), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [An English reading of 12''mo'', which stands for XII''mo'', i. e. L. (''in'') ''duodecimo'': see ''duodecimo.'' Cf. ''sixteenmo.''] Same as ''duodecimo'': commonly written 12''mo.''

'''twelvemonth''' (twelv′munth), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twelfmoneth'', < ''twelmond''; < ''twelve'' + ''month.''] A year, which consists of twelve calendar months.

{{smaller block|A ''twelmond'' & two wekes twynnet we noght.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 13230.}}}}
<poem>I sware a vow before them all, that I,
Because I had not seen the Grail, would ride
A ''twelvemonth'' and a day in quest of it.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}

'''twelvepence''' (twelv′pens), ''n.'' [Orig. two words, ''twelve pence.''] A shilling.

'''twelvepenny''' (twelv′pen″i), ''a.'' '''1.''' Sold for or costing a shilling; worth a shilling.
{{smaller block|When, at a new play, you take up the ''twelve-penny'' room, next the stage. {{right|''Dekker'', Gull’s Hornbook, Proem.}}}}
'''2.''' Hence, of little value; cheap; trifling; insignificant.
{{smaller block|That men be not excommunicated for trifles and ''twelve-penny'' matters.
{{right|''Heylin'', Hist. Presbyterians, p. 371. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''twelve-score''' (twelv′skōr), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Numbering twelve times twenty, or two hundred and forty: as, ''twelve-score'' seamen.

'''II.''' ''n.'' Twelve-score yards, a common length for a shot in archery, and hence often alluded to formerly in measurement.
{{smaller block|I’ll procure this fat rogue a charge of foot; and I know his death will be a march of ''twelve-score.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 598.}}}}

'''Twelve-tide†''', ''n.'' Same as ''Twelfth-tide.''
{{smaller block|Seven night at the lest after ''twelve-tide'' last, on a certaine night he came downe into the parlor, fynding Alice Gedsale & Elizabeth Buppell folding clothes.
{{right|''Darrell Papers'' (H. Hall’s Society in Elizabethan Age,}}
{{right|[App. ii.).}}}}

'''twentieth''' (twen′ti-eth), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''twentith;'' < ME. ''twentithe, twenteothe,'' < AS. ''twentigotha,'' etc., twentieth; as ''twenty'' + ''-eth.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Next after the nineteenth: an ordinal numeral. {{smaller block|January, 1900, but in January, 1901.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 64.}}}}
'''2.''' Being one of twenty equal parts into which anything is divided.

II. ''n.'' '''1.''' The quotient of unity divided by twenty; one of twenty equal parts of anything. —'''2.''' In ''early Eng. law'', a twentieth of the rents of the year, or of movables, or both, granted or levied by way of tax.

'''twenty''' (twen′ti), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''twenty'', ''twenti'', ''twentiȝ'', < AS. ''twentig'', ''twēntig'', ONorth. ''twǣntig'', ''twǣgentig'' = OS. ''twēntig'' = OFries. ''twintich'' = D. ''twintig'' = LG. ''twintig'' = OHG. ''zweinzug'', MHG. ''zwēnzic'', ''zweinzec'', G. ''zwanzig'' = Icel. ''tuttugu'' = Sw. ''tjugu'' = Dan. ''tyve'' = Goth. ''twaitigjus'', twenty; < AS. ''twēgen'', ''twā'', etc., two, + ''-tig'', etc.: see ''twain'' and ''-ty''<sup>1</sup>.] I. ''a.'' '''1.''' One more than nineteen; twice ten: a cardinal numeral.—'''2.''' Proverbially, an indefinite number: sometimes duplicated.
{{smaller block|As for Maximilian, upon ''twenty'' respects he could not have been the man.
{{right|''Bacon'', Hist. Hen. VII., p. 350.}}
I could satisfy myself about ''twenty'' and ''twenty'' things, that now and then I want to know.
{{right|''Richardson'', Sir Charles Grandison, I. xlvii.}}}}

II. ''n.''; pl. ''twenties'' (-tiz). '''1.''' The number which is one more than nineteen; twice ten; a score.—'''2.''' A symbol representing this number, as 20, XX, or xx.—'''3.''' An old division of English infantry (see ''thousand'' and ''hundred''). The commander of a twenty was called ''vintiner''.

'''Twenty-first rule.''' See ''rule''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Twenty-five Articles.''' See ''article''.

'''twenty-fold''' (twen′ti-fōld), ''a.'' [< ''twenty'' + ''-fold''.] Twenty times as many.

'''twenty-four''' (twen′ti-fōr′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Four more than twenty: a cardinal numeral. —{{smaller|'''Twenty-four hours,''' a day, as consisting of so many hours.}}
{{smaller block|Botanists may find it worth while to observe if it [the Martagon lily] smells offensively at any time during the ''twenty-four hours.''
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 193.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The number made up of four and twenty.—'''2.''' A symbol representing this number, as 24, XXIV, or xxiv.—'''3.''' ''pl.'' In ''printing'': (''a'') A form of composed type or plates containing twenty-four pages properly arranged for printing and folding in consecutive order. (''b'') A sheet of paper printed from a form arranged as above described. (''c'') A book made up of sections of twenty-four pages.
{{smaller block|I have observed that the author of a folio . . . sets himself above the author of a quarto; the author of a quarto above the author of an octavo; and so on, by a gradual descent and subordination, to an author in ''twenty-fours.''
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 529.}}}}

''twelvemo'', ''duodecimo'', etc.] '''1.''' A leaf from a sheet of paper regularly folded for a book in twenty-four equal parts. {{smaller|When the size of paper is not named, it is supposed to be a medium 24mo, of which the untrimmed leaf is about 3⅝ by 5¼ inches.}} '''2.''' A book made up of leaves folded in twenty-four equal parts.

Usually written 24''mo''.

'''twentymo''' (twen′ti-mō), ''n.'' [Cf. ''twentyfourmo.''] A sheet regularly folded to make twenty leaves of uniform size. Written shortly 20''mo''. ''C. T. Jacobi'', Printers’ Vocab.

'''twenty-second''' (twen′ti-sek′ond), ''n.'' In ''music'', a tone distant three octaves from a given tone, or the interval between two such tones; a triple octave.

'''’twere''' (twėr). A contraction of ''it were''.
{{smaller block|You are so ridiculously unworthy that ’''twere'' a Folly to reprove you with a serious Look.
{{right|''Etherege'', She-Would if She Could, iv. 2.}}}}

'''twey†''', '''tweyn†''', '''tweyfold†'''. See ''twain'', ''twofold''.

'''twi-'''. [Also ''twy-''; < ME. ''twi-'', < AS. ''twi-'' = OFries. ''twi-'' = D. ''twee-'' = MLG. ''twi-'', ''twe-'', LG. ''twe-'' = OHG. MHG. ''zwi-'', G. ''zwie-'' = Icel. ''tvī'', a combining form of AS. ''twā'', etc., E. ''two'': see ''two'', and cf. ''bi-''<sup>2</sup>, ''di-''<sup>2</sup>.] A prefix of Anglo-Saxon origin, a form of ''two'' in composition. It occurs in ''twibill'', ''twiblade'', ''twifallow'', ''twifold'', ''twilight'', etc.

'''twibill''' (twī′bil), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''twibil'', ''twybill'', ''twybil'', ''twyble''; < ME. ''twibil'', ''twyble'', < AS. ''twibill'', < ''twi-'', two, + ''bill'', a bill: see ''twi-'' and ''bill''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' A double-bladed battle-ax, especially that carried by the Northern nations. {{smaller|Such battle-axes are often mentioned in literature, although but few heads of double axes have been found among thousands of other types. Compare ''Danish ax'' (under ''Danish''), and ''ax''.}}
<poem>At Byzantium many a year ago
My father bore the ''twibil'' valiantly.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 5.}}}} standing of the word. See the quotation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where ''Twibil'' hung, with basket-hilt,
Grown rusty now, but had been gilt.</poem>
{{right|''Cotton'', Scarronides, iv.}}}}
'''3.''' A kind of double ax; a kind of mattock the blade of which has one end shaped like an ax and the other like an adz.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit toles moo
The mattok, ''twyble'', picoys, forth to goo.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 42.}}
<poem>She learn’d the churlish axe and ''twybill'' to prepare,
To steel the coulter’s edge, and sharp the furrowing share.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xviii. 77.}}}}
'''4.''' A mortising-tool.
{{smaller block|A ''twybill'', which is a toole wherewith carpenters make mortaises. ''Nomenclator.'' (''Nares.'')}}
'''5.''' A reaping-hook. ''Drayton.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')—'''6†.''' Same as ''roaring boy'' (see ''roaring'').
{{smaller block|Those lawless ruffians who, to the disgrace of the city, under the various names of Mohawks, . . . ''Twibills'', . . . etc., infested the streets, . . . from the days of Elizabeth down to the beginning of the last century.
{{right|''Gifford'', note in Ford’s Sun’s Darling, i. 1.}}}}

'''twibilled''' (twī′bild), ''a.'' [< ''twibill'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Armed with a twibill or twibills.
{{smaller block|<poem>But if in this reign
The halberted train
Or the constable should rebel,
And make this ''twybill’d'' militia to swell.</poem>
{{right|''Loyal Songs.'' (''Mason’s Supp. to Johnson.'')}}}}

'''twiblade''' (twī′blād), ''n.'' [Also ''twyblade''; < ''twi-'' + ''blade''.] Same as ''twayblade''.

'''twice''' (twīs), ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. ''twise''; < ME. ''twies'', ''twiȝes'', < AS. ''twiges'' (= MLG. ''twiges'', ''twies'' = MHG. ''zwies''), with adv. gen. ''-es'', < AS. ''twiwa'', ME. ''twie'', twice: see ''twie''.] '''1.''' Two times; on two occasions; in two instances.
{{smaller block|That Cytee was wont to be righte strong; but it was ''twyes'' wonnen of the Cristene Men.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 46.}}
<poem>Thus ''twyes'' in his slepynge dremed he.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 192.}}
What, would’st thou have a serpent sting thee ''twice?''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' In twofold degree or quantity; doubly.
{{smaller block|Their arrowes an ell long, which they will shoot ''twice'' as fast as our men. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 844.}}
If any Stranger be desirous to bring away any for Novelty’s sake, he must be a great Favourite to get a pair of Shoes of them [Chinese women], though he give ''twice'' their value. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 408.}}
<poem>And, if you asked of him to say
What ''twice'' 10 was, or 3 times 7,
He’d glance (in quite a placid way)
From heaven to earth, from earth to heaven.</poem>
{{right|''C. S. Calverley'', Gemini and Virgo.}}}}

'''At twice.''' (''a'') At two distinct times; by two distinct operations.
{{smaller block|<poem>He took out an Instrument, bored thirty holes ''at twice'',
As they sailed to the Lowlands low.</poem>
{{right|''Ballad of the Goulden Vanitee'', quoted in Mrs. Gordon’s}}
{{right|[Christopher North, p. 433.}}
“Did Mr. Tulliver let you have the money all at once?” said Mrs. Tulliver. . . . “No; ''at twice'',” said Mrs. Moss.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, iii. 3.}}
His Grace should have . . . a glass and a half of Champagne. His Grace won’t drink his wine out of a tumbler, so perhaps your ladyship won’t mind giving it him ''at twice''. {{right|''Trollope'', Phineas Redux, xxv.}}}}
(''b'') The second time; by or on a second trial, performance, etc.
{{smaller block|I could hardly compasse one of them [pillars] ''at twice'' with both my armes. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 220.}}}}
<poem>Please but your worship now
To take three drops of the rich water with you,
I’ll undertake your man shall cure you, sir,
''At twice'' i’ your own chamber.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, iv. 2.}}}}

'''Twice-laid rope.''' See ''rope''<sup>1</sup>.

'''twice†''' (twīs), ''a.'' [< ''twice, adv.''] Occurring twice.
{{smaller block|And, more to our sorrow, we heard of the ''twice'' returne of the Paragon, that now the third time was sent vs three moneths agoe.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 236.}}}}

{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 4. 108.}}}}
